toc.title: Prescribed movement versus following the body
What might have been going on for Z
The experience matters more than the movement

blocks.p: I got a question from someone on YouTube who left it in the comments, and I want to address it here. It's about flight, fight, shutdown, TRE exercises, and what went wrong.

I'll call this person Z. Z says: "I used to live in fight or flight response with severe anxiety and DPDR. So I did excessive TRE exercises, and now I feel numb. No more anxiety (flight or fight). And my head feels weird. Can you tell me what I can do to get back to fight or flight where I can do relaxation techniques again? Because now I can't do them anymore. Also, can you shed light on what happened to me? I'm confused."
No, I can't tell you exactly what happened to you, and no, I can't tell you exactly what you should do. But I can approach this generally. That's my attempt here.

blocks.h: Prescribed movement versus following the body

blocks.p: I have some familiarity with TRE exercises. I'm not a proponent of them. I don't know a ton, so take that for what it's worth. But the way I approach mental health and trauma recovery is, I think, different.

This could be coming from a very uneducated viewpoint, but rather than looking at our trauma as something we need to resolve through some sort of prescribed movement, I look at it like this: first we build lots and lots of safety. Then we gently feel into our stuck defense a little bit at a time, and relieve it a little bit at a time. And then, if our body wants to move, we move.

I just finished a small cohort that helps someone come out of shutdown and emerge into sympathetic activation, which I think has a lot to do with what's being asked here. In our mindful practices, I didn't tell people how to move around. I didn't give them any prescribed movements. Instead, we anchored into safety, and then mindfully felt into stuck defensive activation, into immobilization. Then, to wrap up the meditation and the brief pendulation exercise, we asked our body what would feel good right now. And then we moved in a way that felt good.

One of the people stretched out a couple of times. The final time we met, I think, she did this swimming motion. The other person grabbed a pillow and squeezed it. These are not movements I can predict. I don't know what the right movement is for anybody.

Again, this may be a very uneducated place to speak from, and I apologize if it is, but I believe TRE exercises are more prescribed, like "do this movement." If I'm wrong about that, I apologize. I've looked into it, but not heavily. If I'm understanding it correctly, it's fundamentally at odds with the way I do things.

blocks.h: What might have been going on for Z

blocks.p: So let's get back to Z's question. Z had fight or flight, plus DPDR. I would guess DPDR comes from a severe or significant enough shutdown state. Shutdown brings dissociation. So if we're in a depersonalized, derealized sort of state, that must have some degree of dissociation to it, and that comes from shutdown or freeze.

So if somebody has fight or flight and shutdown, they could alternate between the two. That would probably look more like shutdown to fight, shutdown to fight, shutdown to fight. Or it could be shutdown to a brief flight, and then to more anxiety. And that's where someone gets stuck, so they go back down: shutdown, to fight, to flight, to fight, to shutdown. Maybe it could be something like that.

Or they could have both of these things active at the same time: shutdown and fight or flight, maybe more flight active. That would result in a tense kind of freeze state that just lingers chronically. Maybe there's an underlying sense of panic that's always there, or an underlying sense of anxiety. If it's more freeze, I'd lean more toward panic, but an underlying intense anxiety definitely could be there.
So just to understand what could be going on in general: someone with fight or flight and DPDR might have lingering freeze, or they might be going shutdown to sympathetic, shutdown to sympathetic.

Knowing that is very important, and it's why I don't like the prescribed method of "just do this movement," or "go jump in a cold pool," or "do this breathing method." Knowing what state you're in is more helpful than just throwing these skills at somebody.

Let's say someone is in shutdown, or going from shutdown to sympathetic. Someone in shutdown is way less likely to do any sort of movement. They need very small movements. Maybe TRE has small movements built in that are good. I don't know.

But the way I work with someone in shutdown, instead of trying to get into fight activation or trying to work our way out of shutdown, we actually connect with the shutdown. We let it be, because it's there anyway. So let's mindfully connect with it. Once we mindfully connect with it, self-regulation can happen naturally, as long as the safety state is strengthened enough.
So for someone in shutdown, throwing some sort of movement at them is not necessarily helpful, unless it's tailored to what their body wants, and it's probably a smaller movement.

Someone in flight or fight has more capacity for movement. They probably have more range of movement. But they're probably going to be more on the tense side. Not like freeze, but their willingness, their playfulness when it comes to movement, is going to be smaller.

So yes, they might be able to roll around or something like that, but they're probably going to be thinking, "This is stupid. Why am I doing this?" Or, "This isn't working for me. It works for everybody else, but it won't work for me." And if that's true, I don't think they're going to benefit from the movement. I have no idea how much mindfulness is built into TRE, or how much safety is expected.

Someone in freeze has flight and fight active, but also shutdown. So they're mobile, but that mobility is frozen. It's immobilized by the shutdown aspect of the freeze. They're mobile and immobile at the same time.

If I asked someone in freeze to do some sort of prescribed movement, and they lacked the safety to benefit from it, their system may not have the capacity for it, because the immobility aspect of the freeze is too strong. I could totally see this person really struggling with any sort of movement-based, mindfulness-based kind of stuff. I think someone in freeze could definitely be triggered deeper into shutdown, or even deeper into freeze.

And someone in freeze who has successfully removed the shutdown, the immobility of their freeze, still may not be at a place where they can handle mindful movement, because their safety state isn't where it needs to be. There are a lot of pieces that come into this. That's why I hate to prescribe stuff.

Let's say someone in freeze has been able to connect with the shutdown immobilization, and now the mobilization, the flight and fight, is ready to be released. That can be extremely difficult. That can be a lot, especially if their safety state can't handle it.

Think of it as your foot being on the brake and the gas at the same time. Not a little bit: floored. So when you take your foot off the brake, what happens? You're going to spin out, right? You might shoot forward, out of control.

It's a metaphor, but it's the same thing with freeze. We don't want that person spinning out or shooting out of control when their immobility comes off. It has to be a little bit at a time, with the safety state active.

blocks.h: The experience matters more than the movement

blocks.p: If I were doing something like this, I would really want to make sure my client is anchored in safety first. Then, ideally, listen to whatever movement their body naturally wants. But if it were a prescribed movement, I would really want my client anchored in safety, and then mindfully feeling the experience of the movement.

I'd be more concerned with what's happening than with completing the movement. If the goal is to roll around on the floor, and I'm making stuff up, I don't know what TRE does, I don't care if they roll around the right number of times or in the right way. I'm way more concerned with the experience of rolling around.

So as soon as their brain says something like "This is stupid, this doesn't work for me," that to me is far more important than completing the movement. I'd want them to pause. Let's notice that thought. What's the emotion driving that thought? Let's just be with that emotion. If we can be with it, and then balance it out with more safety, then we can go back to the exercise if needed.

That's how I work. I'm more concerned with the present moment experience of whatever the thing is. Let's focus on that present moment experience, because that is the portal to actual self-regulation, not just doing things here and there that kind of feel better but don't really last.
And again, I'm not trying to dis TRE. A lot of people love this stuff, and I'm happy for you. The way I work is just fundamentally different from a lot of the other things out there, and that's okay.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Z says, "My head feels weird." I'm not going to comment on that. "What can I do to get back to fight or flight?"

I'll give you the annoying answer. The annoying answer is: don't try to get back to fight or flight. Let's connect with whatever's happening in your body right now. And if the body's ready to get back to fight or flight, it will.
I know that's the annoying answer, but it is the answer, I'm sorry to say.

And this is not just for Z. This is for all of us. It's totally okay to not be content with where you're at. I think it's a good sign. It's totally okay to want to get into sympathetic activation if you're in shutdown. Absolutely. It's totally okay to want more safety in your life. Heck yes.

But I don't believe we can truly get to more safety, or work our way up the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), until we've mindfully connected with what we have in the present moment. And what we have in the present moment might be a lot of collapse.

So the way I work is: let's mindfully connect with the collapse. Let's give it permission to be. If we can do that and remain anchored in safety, if we can mindfully and deeply feel what it's like to be collapsed, then self-regulation will naturally unfold, as long as you're anchored in safety and mindfully tracking and following the natural little sensations and impulses. And we can use skills like balancing and pendulation.
So let's not worry about getting to where we need to be. Let's just be where we're at. If we can connect with where we're at, the body will take you to the next place. It will, I promise.

But it requires a lot of safety, and I think that's the piece people know but skip over. They just want the thing. Just tell me the thing. Tell me the skill, the exercise, the movement, the breathing technique. Just get me out of the state I'm in.
I don't blame anybody for feeling that way or thinking that way at all. But there's no hack. There's no shortcut here. I'm pretty darn sure there is no shortcut.

So the sooner you can focus on and prioritize safety, the sooner you can do even small safety practices every day, the more success you're going to have. That's what I would argue, and it's what I see in myself and in my clients. The safety state is the foundation for everything. The stronger your safety state, the more you'll be able to do the more difficult stuff I'm talking about, like mindfully allowing and feeling shutdown, or flight and fight, or whatever is happening in your system currently.
